items.prompt: Which financial statement reports a company's assets, liabilities and equity at a single point in time?

options.label: Cash flow statement
Income statement
Statement of retained earnings
Balance sheet

rubric: The balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity at one date.
The income statement and cash flow statement cover a period, which is the common confusion.

items.prompt: What is the formula for the current ratio?

options.label: Current assets / current liabilities
Current liabilities / current assets
Total debt / total equity
Net income / revenue

rubric: Current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities.
Inverting it or using leverage or margin formulas confuses liquidity with other ratios.

items.prompt: Which ratio is calculated as net income divided by revenue?

options.label: Debt-to-equity ratio
Net profit margin
Current ratio
Inventory turnover

rubric: Net income over revenue is the net profit margin.
The others measure liquidity, leverage and efficiency.

items.prompt: Which section of the cash flow statement includes cash received from customers for sales?

options.label: Investing activities
Operating activities
Financing activities
Equity activities

rubric: Cash from customers is an operating cash flow.
Investing covers asset purchases and financing covers debt and equity, which learners sometimes mix up.

items.prompt: What does the debt-to-equity ratio compare?

options.label: Current assets to current liabilities
Total liabilities to shareholders' equity
Total assets to total revenue
Net income to shareholders' equity

rubric: Debt-to-equity compares liabilities (debt) with shareholders' equity.
Net income to equity is ROE, and current assets to current liabilities is the current ratio.

items.prompt: Which of the following are line items found on an income statement? Select all that apply.

options.label: Accounts payable
Cost of goods sold
Retained earnings
Revenue
Net income

rubric: Revenue, cost of goods sold and net income are income statement items.
Accounts payable and retained earnings are balance sheet items.

items.prompt: A new analyst is asked to find out how much profit a company earned over the last year after all expenses and taxes. She has the balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement in front of her. Which line should she look for?

options.label: Ending cash on the cash flow statement
Total assets on the balance sheet
Net income on the income statement
Total equity on the balance sheet

rubric: Net income is the profit after all expenses and taxes, shown on the income statement.
Equity, cash and assets are not measures of period profit.

items.prompt: A company's current ratio rises from 1.2 to 2.0 over a year. What does this most directly suggest?

options.label: Its short-term liquidity has improved
Its profitability has improved sharply
Its long-term debt burden has fallen
Its sales growth has accelerated

rubric: A higher current ratio means more current assets per dollar of current liabilities, so better liquidity.
The ratio says nothing directly about profit, debt or sales growth.

items.prompt: Why can a company report positive net income but still have negative operating cash flow?

options.label: Net income counts only transactions settled in cash
Revenue may be recorded before the cash is collected
Operating cash flow leaves out revenue from credit sales
Profit is always paid out as dividends before it is counted

rubric: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned, so customers may not have paid yet.
Net income is not cash-based, which is the misconception in the distractors.

items.prompt: Company A has a net profit margin of 4% and Company B has 12%, both in the same industry. What does this indicate?

options.label: B holds more cash on its balance sheet than A does
B earns more total revenue than A does each year
B keeps more profit from each dollar of revenue
B carries less debt relative to its equity than A

rubric: Margin shows profit per dollar of revenue, so B keeps more of each dollar.
Margin does not reveal revenue size, debt or cash.

items.prompt: A company's debt-to-equity ratio increases from 0.5 to 1.5. How should this be interpreted?

options.label: Its cash balance has tripled
It is relying more on borrowed funds relative to owners' funds
Its profits have tripled
It is relying more on owners' funds relative to borrowed funds

rubric: A higher ratio means more debt per dollar of equity, so higher leverage.
Reading it as less debt or as profit growth misinterprets the ratio.

items.prompt: Why do analysts compare several years of statements rather than a single year?

options.label: To confirm that the accounting equation holds
To remove the need for ratios
To make all firms identical in size
To reveal trends that one year cannot show

rubric: Trend analysis shows direction and consistency over time.
Trends complement ratios and do not replace them or check the accounting equation.

items.prompt: Which of the following would generally be interpreted as signs of stronger profitability? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rising return on assets
Rising net profit margin
Rising gross margin
Rising debt-to-equity ratio
Falling current ratio

rubric: Higher margins and higher return on equity indicate stronger profitability.
Debt-to-equity and current ratio measure leverage and liquidity, not profitability.

items.prompt: A small retailer reports revenue of $500,000 and net income of $50,000 this year. Last year it reported revenue of $400,000 and net income of $60,000. The owner says the business did better because revenue grew. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: Revenue grew 25%, so sales momentum shows profitability improved even though net income dipped slightly
Net income fell only $10,000, which is small next to the $100,000 revenue gain, so results are about the same
Both revenue and margin rose from last year, so profitability clearly improved
Margin fell from 15% to 10%, so profitability weakened despite higher revenue

rubric: Margin fell from 60/400 = 15% to 50/500 = 10%, so profitability weakened despite higher revenue.
Looking only at revenue growth hides the margin decline.

items.prompt: A company reports a current ratio of 2.0. What does this tell you?

options.label: Annual revenue is twice as large as current liabilities
Cash on hand is twice as large as current liabilities
Total assets are twice as large as total liabilities
Current assets are twice as large as current liabilities

rubric: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities, so 2.0 means twice as many.
Distractors swap in total assets, revenue or cash, which are not what the ratio uses.

items.prompt: Why is a company's net profit margin usually lower than its gross margin?

options.label: Net margin leaves out the cost of goods sold completely
Gross margin adds back interest and taxes to the profit figure
Net margin also deducts operating expenses, interest and taxes
Net margin uses a much larger revenue figure than gross margin

rubric: Net income is what remains after operating costs, interest and tax as well as cost of goods sold.
Distractors misstate the revenue base or which costs each margin includes.

items.prompt: A firm shows positive net income but negative operating cash flow. Which explanation is most plausible?

options.label: Dividends paid to owners are deducted in operating cash flow
Sales were booked as revenue but customers have not yet paid
Net income counts only cash sales, so it is always accurate
Depreciation is a large cash payment that lowers only income

rubric: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned, so unpaid receivables raise income but not cash.
Distractors misdescribe depreciation, dividends or what net income includes.

items.prompt: A company's debt-to-equity ratio rises from 0.8 to 1.4 over two years. What does this most directly indicate?

options.label: It collects payments from customers more quickly than before
It earns more profit on each dollar of sales than before
It is financing more of its assets with borrowed money
It holds more cash relative to what it owes in the short term

rubric: A higher debt-to-equity ratio means greater reliance on debt relative to owners' funds.
Distractors confuse leverage with profitability, receivables collection or liquidity.

items.prompt: What does trend (horizontal) analysis of an income statement mainly show?

options.label: How the firm's ratios compare with a competitor's ratios in the same year
How much cash the firm holds at a single balance sheet date
How each expense compares to total revenue within one year
How a line item such as revenue changes across several periods

rubric: Horizontal analysis tracks the same item over time.
Distractors describe common-size (vertical) analysis, peer comparison or a point-in-time balance.

items.prompt: Which of the following ratios mainly measure a company's liquidity? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cash ratio
Quick ratio
Debt-to-equity ratio
Current ratio
Return on equity

rubric: Current, quick and cash ratios compare liquid assets with short-term obligations.
Return on equity measures profitability and debt-to-equity measures leverage.

items.prompt: A retailer's revenue rose 10% this year, but its net income fell 5%. The notes mention no unusual one-off items. What is the most reasonable interpretation?

options.label: The company repaid a large part of its borrowings, which cut profit
Operating cash flow fell by about the same percentage as net income
Revenue growth normally lifts profit, so the income statement likely has an error
Costs grew faster than revenue, so the profit margin narrowed

rubric: If profit falls while sales rise, expenses rose faster than revenue and margins shrank.
Distractors assume profit must track revenue, or invent links to cash flow or debt.

items.prompt: A company has current assets of 120,000 and current liabilities of 80,000. What is its current ratio?
rubric: 0.67 comes from inverting the ratio.

items.prompt: A firm has revenue of 600,000 and net income of 45,000. What is its net profit margin?
rubric: 13.3% comes from dividing revenue by income; the others are decimal slips.

items.prompt: A company has total liabilities of 300,000 and shareholders' equity of 200,000. Using debt-to-equity = total liabilities / shareholders' equity, what is its debt-to-equity ratio?
rubric: 2.5 uses total assets over equity; 0.67 inverts the ratio.

items.prompt: A firm has cash 20,000, receivables 30,000, inventory 50,000 and current liabilities 40,000. What is its quick ratio?
rubric: Quick ratio = (cash + receivables) / current liabilities = 50,000 / 40,000 = 1.25.
2.5 wrongly includes inventory; the others use only part of the quick assets.

items.prompt: Revenue grew from 400,000 last year to 460,000 this year. What is the percentage growth?
rubric: 13% uses the new year as the base; 60% is the raw change.

items.prompt: A firm has revenue 500, cost of goods sold 300, operating expenses 100, interest 20 and tax 16 (all in thousands). Which calculations are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Operating margin is 20%
Net margin is 12.8%
Gross margin is 60%
Net margin is 20%
Gross margin is 40%

rubric: Gross profit 200 gives 40%; operating income 100 gives 20%; net income 64 gives 12.8%.
20% net margin ignores interest and tax; 60% uses the cost ratio.

items.prompt: An analyst compares two firms. Firm A has net income of 50 and total assets of 500. Firm B has net income of 30 and total assets of 200 (in millions). The analyst wants to know which uses its assets more efficiently to produce profit. Which conclusion is correct?

options.label: Firm A, because it has more assets available to generate income
Firm B, because its smaller income is easier to grow in future
Firm B, because 30/200 = 15% is higher than 50/500 = 10%
Firm A, because its net income of 50 is larger than 30

rubric: Return on assets: B earns 15% versus A's 10%, so B uses assets better.
Distractors judge by absolute income or asset size instead of the ratio.

items.prompt: A firm reports current assets of 480,000, of which inventory is 180,000, and current liabilities of 240,000. What is its quick ratio (inventory excluded)?
rubric: 2.00 is the current ratio, which keeps inventory in.

items.prompt: A company has net income of 90,000, average total assets of 1,200,000 and average shareholders' equity of 400,000. What is its return on equity?
rubric: 7.5% is ROA, which uses assets in the denominator.

items.prompt: Revenue was 800,000 last year and 920,000 this year. Cost of goods sold was 480,000 last year and 598,000 this year. What was this year's gross margin?
rubric: 40% is last year's margin; 65% is the cost ratio.

items.prompt: A firm has EBIT of 600,000 and interest expense of 150,000. Total debt is 1,500,000 and total equity is 1,000,000. What is its interest coverage ratio?
rubric: Interest coverage = EBIT / interest = 600,000 / 150,000 = 4.0x.
2.5x is debt-to-equity inverted or mixed up with a leverage figure.

items.prompt: Annual credit sales are 3,650,000 and year-end accounts receivable are 500,000 (use 365 days and year-end balances). What are the days sales outstanding?

options.label: 50 days
7.3 days
73 days
36.5 days

rubric: 73 days comes from using 7.3 turnover inverted incorrectly; others are scaling slips.

items.prompt: A firm has total debt of 600,000, total equity of 400,000 and total assets of 1,000,000. Which of these ratios are computed correctly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Debt-to-assets is 60%
Debt-to-equity is 1.5
Debt-to-equity is 0.67
Equity multiplier is 2.5

rubric: 0.67 inverts the debt-to-equity ratio.

items.prompt: An analyst is checking a retailer. Net income is 50,000, depreciation is 30,000, accounts receivable rose by 20,000, inventory fell by 10,000, and accounts payable rose by 15,000. No other operating items changed. Using the indirect method, what is cash flow from operations?
rubric: 65,000 or 105,000 come from reversing the sign of working capital changes.

items.prompt: A company's net income rose 25% but cash flow from operations fell 30% in the same year. Receivables and inventory both grew much faster than sales. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: Earnings are being tied up in working capital rather than collected
The firm repaid long-term debt, which reduced its operating cash flow
Profit margins fell sharply, so reported net income should have declined
Depreciation expense rose sharply, which lowered both income and cash flow

rubric: Growing receivables and inventory absorb cash while income is still recognised.
Debt repayment is a financing flow, not operating.

items.prompt: ROE rose from 12% to 18% while net profit margin and asset turnover stayed unchanged. Using the DuPont breakdown, what must have changed?

options.label: Financial leverage rose
Tax rate dropped
Operating costs fell
Inventory turnover improved

rubric: ROE = margin x turnover x equity multiplier, so with the first two fixed leverage must have risen.
Cost or tax changes would alter margin.

items.prompt: Two firms both have a current ratio of 2.0. Firm A holds mostly cash and receivables. Firm B holds mostly slow-moving inventory. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: Firm A is more liquid because its assets convert to cash faster
Firm B is more liquid because its inventory is carried at a higher book value
Firm B is safer because inventory can be sold at cost to meet short-term debts
They are equally liquid because the current ratios are identical

rubric: Composition of current assets matters, so quick liquidity differs.
Equal ratios do not imply equal liquidity.

items.prompt: A firm's operating margin is stable, but its net margin fell sharply. Revenue and gross margin are unchanged. Which line item is the most logical place to look first?

options.label: Selling and admin expenses
Cost of goods sold
Depreciation and amortization
Interest expense and taxes

rubric: Stable operating margin means the decline arose below operating income.
COGS, selling and admin expenses, and depreciation and amortization are all above that line.

items.prompt: A company's inventory turnover dropped from 8 to 5 while sales stayed flat and cost of goods sold stayed flat. What does this indicate?

options.label: The company is selling inventory faster than before
Receivables collection has slowed
Inventory balances grew relative to the cost of sales
Cost of goods sold must have risen

rubric: Turnover = COGS / inventory; flat COGS and lower turnover means higher inventory.
Receivables is a separate measure.

items.prompt: A firm shows strong net income but negative free cash flow for three years. Which findings would best support the view that earnings quality is a concern? Select all that apply.

options.label: Operating cash flow consistently well below net income
Receivables growing faster than revenue
Rising days inventory outstanding
Capital spending well above depreciation, funded by new long-term debt

rubric: Receivables build-up, inventory build-up and a persistent gap between income and operating cash are earnings quality flags.
Heavy growth capex alone explains negative FCF without implying poor earnings quality.

items.prompt: An analyst compares two years for a manufacturer. Sales grew 10%, but operating income grew 2%. Gross margin was unchanged, while administrative and selling expenses rose 25%. The CFO says pricing pressure caused the weaker profit growth. Which assessment is best supported by the data?

options.label: Pricing pressure is confirmed, since profit grew slower than sales did
Raw material costs rose faster than prices, since profit lagged sales growth
Higher interest expense is the cause, since it reduced profit growth below sales growth
Overhead growth, not pricing, explains it, as gross margin held steady

rubric: Unchanged gross margin rules out pricing or material cost problems; the opex rise explains it.
Interest is below operating income so cannot affect it.

items.prompt: A firm reports net income up 20% year on year. Operating cash flow is flat, and accounts receivable rose 45% on revenue growth of 8%. Which explanation fits these figures best?

options.label: Reported profit growth is being driven by sales on credit that have not yet been collected in cash
The firm has repaid long-term debt, which lowered interest expense and reduced operating cash
The firm has cut its cost of goods sold through better supplier terms and so keeps more cash
Depreciation expense has risen sharply and has reduced net income below true cash earnings

rubric: Receivables growing far faster than revenue while cash flow lags points to credit sales or loose recognition inflating profit.
Distractors attribute the gap to cost or financing effects that would not inflate receivables.

items.prompt: A distributor's current ratio rose from 1.2 to 1.6, yet its quick ratio fell from 0.9 to 0.6 over the same year. What most likely happened?

options.label: Long-term debt was reclassified as current, which raised current liabilities and the current ratio
Inventory grew faster than cash and receivables, so liquidity became weaker than the current ratio suggests
Receivables were collected faster, which raised cash and strengthened immediate liquidity
Short-term borrowing was repaid with cash, which lowered current liabilities and the quick ratio

rubric: Quick ratio excludes inventory, so a rising current ratio with a falling quick ratio signals an inventory build-up.
Other options would move both ratios in the same direction.

items.prompt: A company's ROE rose from 12% to 18%. Its net profit margin and total asset turnover were unchanged. Which driver in a DuPont decomposition explains the rise?

options.label: A higher equity multiplier, for example from debt-funded share buybacks that shrank equity
A higher tax burden, because lower tax rates leave more profit for shareholders
A higher interest burden, because the firm cut costs and kept more of its operating profit
A higher operating margin, because pricing power improved while the net margin stayed the same

rubric: With margin and turnover fixed, only leverage can raise ROE.
Tax, interest and operating margin changes would alter net margin, which was stated as unchanged.

items.prompt: A firm's interest coverage (EBIT / interest expense) fell from 6x to 2.5x. Its debt balance and interest expense were unchanged. What does this show?

options.label: Net debt rose through lower cash balances, which weakened the coverage calculation
The firm's tax rate rose, which lowered the profit left to cover interest payments
The firm refinanced at a higher rate, which raised its interest expense and cut coverage
Operating profit fell, so earnings available to cover the same interest bill shrank

rubric: Interest expense is constant, so the numerator, EBIT, must have fallen.
Distractors change interest or use post-tax items that EBIT coverage excludes.

items.prompt: A retailer's gross margin held at 40% for three years, but its operating margin fell from 12% to 7%. Where should an analyst look first?

options.label: Operating expenses such as selling and administrative costs growing faster than revenue
The inventory valuation method, because it changes gross margin from year to year
Product pricing and supplier costs, because they drive the cost of goods sold
Interest expense on borrowings, because it sits between gross profit and operating profit

rubric: Stable gross margin means the gap opens below gross profit, in operating expenses.
Interest is below operating profit, and COGS-related causes would move gross margin.

items.prompt: Which observations suggest a company's earnings quality is deteriorating? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cash rose after a planned equity issue to fund expansion
Dividends rose modestly while the payout ratio stayed stable
Days sales outstanding keeps rising while revenue growth slows
A one-off asset sale gain makes up a large share of this year's profit
Operating cash flow has been well below net income for several years

rubric: Rising DSO, persistent cash shortfall and non-recurring gains all show profit not backed by repeatable cash.
A stable payout and a planned equity raise do not indicate weaker earnings quality.

items.prompt: An analyst compares two retailers. Retailer A has inventory turnover of 4x and gross margin of 45%. Retailer B has inventory turnover of 8x and gross margin of 25%. Both have return on assets of about 9%. What best explains how both earn similar returns?

options.label: Retailer B must be understating its costs, since a gross margin that low cannot produce the same return on assets as a higher-margin rival
Inventory turnover and gross margin are unrelated to return on assets, so the matching returns are a coincidence of the two firms' accounting
Retailer A is less efficient overall, so its higher margin only offsets weaker inventory management and the firms are not truly comparable
Retailer A earns more per sale while Retailer B turns stock faster, so each reaches a similar return by a different route

rubric: Return on assets combines margin and turnover, so different strategies can give equal returns.
Distractors assume that a single ratio determines performance.

items.prompt: A lender assesses a capital-intensive manufacturer whose maintenance capex is large and recurring. The lender wants the metric that best shows ability to meet debt payments from operations. Which should it weight most?

options.label: Total revenue divided by total assets, because it shows how fully assets are used
EBITDA divided by interest expense, since it removes non-cash charges
Operating cash flow less capex, divided by scheduled debt service
Net income divided by total debt, because it reflects profit after all costs

rubric: Cash left after required reinvestment, relative to debt service, matches the stated need.
EBITDA ignores heavy capex, and the other options are not payment-capacity measures.

items.prompt: An analyst compares the operating profitability of two firms with very different debt levels. The goal is to ignore financing choices. Which metric is the best fit?

options.label: Return on equity, because it measures what shareholders earn
Earnings per share, because it scales profit to the share count
Net profit margin, because it captures every cost the firm bears
After-tax operating profit divided by invested capital

rubric: NOPAT over invested capital excludes capital structure effects.
ROE, net margin and EPS are all distorted by interest and leverage.

items.prompt: A firm lengthened the useful lives of its equipment, which raised reported operating profit. An analyst must compare it with peers on a basis unaffected by that change. Which measure is most reliable?

options.label: Return on assets, because it adjusts for the size of the asset base
Earnings per share, because it is audited each year
Operating profit margin, because it includes all operating costs
Operating cash flow, because depreciation is a non-cash charge

rubric: Operating cash flow does not depend on depreciation estimates.
Margin, EPS and ROA all use profit figures that the longer lives inflate.

items.prompt: A colleague argues a company is safe because its current ratio is 2.5. Most current assets are slow-moving inventory, and large debt matures in six months. What is the best critique?

options.label: The claim is sound, because a current ratio above 2 normally signals a strong liquidity cushion
The claim is weak, because the ratio ignores asset quality and the timing of debt maturities
The claim is weak, because current ratio is distorted by debt and should be replaced with debt-to-equity
The claim is sound, because inventory is recorded at cost and is usually sold at book value within the year

rubric: Liquidity depends on how quickly assets convert to cash relative to when obligations fall due.
Distractors rely on rule-of-thumb thresholds or assume inventory converts at book value.

items.prompt: A firm's net margin rose for three years, and management says profitability is improving. Over the same period it made large acquisitions and its ROIC fell. Which assessment is best supported?

options.label: Profitability improved, because margin is the standard measure of how well a firm earns
The result is neutral, because acquisitions affect the balance sheet rather than returns
Value creation weakened, since margin ignores the larger capital base now needed to earn the profit
The ROIC decline is irrelevant, because it is calculated using a different accounting period

rubric: Returns on capital show whether new investment earns its cost; margin alone cannot.
Distractors treat margin as sufficient or dismiss capital employed.

items.prompt: A subscription software firm bills annual contracts upfront and is growing fast. Which are valid reasons to weight cash flow measures alongside net income when judging it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cash flow can't be affected by working capital changes such as deferred revenue
Net income may be depressed by heavy customer acquisition spending that is expensed
Cash flow figures are never influenced by management timing of payments
Cash flow shows whether growth is self-funding or reliant on outside capital
Upfront billing raises operating cash flow ahead of revenue recognition

rubric: Deferred revenue, expensed acquisition costs and funding needs make cash flow informative alongside profit.
Cash flow is affected by working capital and by timing choices, so those options are wrong.

items.prompt: An investor must choose one of two firms for a conservative portfolio. The criteria are stable cash generation and downside protection. Firm X has a P/E of 8, debt of 5x EBITDA and negative free cash flow. Firm Y has a P/E of 16, debt of 1x EBITDA and positive free cash flow each year. Which choice best meets the criteria?

options.label: Firm Y, because positive free cash flow and low leverage support stability despite the higher P/E
Neither, because a P/E far from the market average shows earnings are unreliable for either firm
Firm X, because high leverage magnifies returns on equity and so improves protection in a downturn
Firm X, because the low P/E means the price is cheap relative to earnings, giving the largest margin of safety

rubric: The stated criteria are cash stability and protection, which favour Y's cash flow and low debt.
A low P/E on a leveraged, cash-burning firm can signal distress rather than safety.

items.prompt: A distributor's operating margin is stable, but its cash conversion cycle lengthened from 45 to 80 days over two years while revenue grew 30%. Judging by cash generation quality, which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: The stable operating margin shows cash generation is stable, since margins capture all operating efficiency
Growth is consuming working capital, so reported earnings overstate the cash the business is really generating
Revenue growth of 30% proves demand is healthy, so a longer cycle is a minor accounting timing matter that will reverse
The longer cycle shows stronger supplier terms, which should raise free cash flow over time

rubric: A longer cycle with fast growth ties cash up in receivables and inventory, so earnings outrun cash.
Distractors treat margin as a proxy for cash or read a lengthening cycle as favorable.

items.prompt: Two retailers have identical net income and debt/equity of 1.0. Firm A leases its stores under operating leases kept off the debt figure; Firm B owns stores financed by mortgages shown as debt. Which judgement about comparing leverage is best?

options.label: Firm B is more leveraged, because mortgage borrowings are recorded obligations while lease payments are ordinary rent expenses
Firm A is probably more levered than shown, because fixed lease commitments act like debt and should be added
The firms are equally levered, because identical debt/equity ratios reflect the same claims on the firms' assets and income
Firm A is less leveraged, because lease payments are operating costs that are usually not treated as debt service

rubric: Leases create fixed obligations like debt; adjusting makes the comparison fair.
Distractors rely on the reported ratio without adjusting for financing form.

items.prompt: An analyst ranks four firms on ROE. Firm X has the highest ROE at 28%, driven by a DuPont breakdown of 3% net margin, 1.2 asset turnover and 7.8 equity multiplier. For judging durable profitability, what is the best critique?

options.label: The high equity multiplier is a strength, because extra debt raises shareholder returns and the interest cost is covered by the asset turnover
The thin margin is the main concern, since turnover and the equity multiplier are fixed features of the industry and say little about ROE quality
ROE is mostly leverage-driven, so it is fragile; judge it against margin and risk
ROE is reliable here because a figure above 20% usually signals strong management, whatever the mix of drivers behind it

rubric: DuPont shows ROE built on leverage with a thin margin, raising risk.
Distractors treat ROE level or leverage as inherently good.

items.prompt: A software firm reports rising net income, but operating cash flow is flat and deferred revenue is falling sharply. The criterion is the reliability of future revenue growth. Which interpretation is most defensible?

options.label: Falling deferred revenue means customers are paying faster, which is a liquidity improvement and shows stronger collections
Falling deferred revenue signals weakening new billings, so future recognized revenue likely slows despite current income
Rising net income confirms revenue momentum, so deferred revenue changes are only a presentation matter within liabilities
Flat operating cash flow is normal for software firms, so it carries no information about earnings quality or revenue

rubric: Deferred revenue is a leading indicator of future recognized revenue.
Distractors misread the liability as a payment-speed or presentation item.

items.prompt: A firm's current ratio rose from 1.2 to 2.0 in a year. Receivables days rose by 40, inventory turnover halved, and cash fell. Judging liquidity quality, which statement is best?

options.label: Liquidity improved, because the higher ratio shows more current assets relative to short-term liabilities, so obligations are better covered
Liquidity is probably weaker than the ratio implies, because the rise is in slower-converting assets, not cash
Liquidity is unaffected, since receivables and inventory are both counted at book value in the current ratio, so the mix of assets cannot matter
Liquidity improved, since any current ratio above 1.5 shows ample ability to meet short-term obligations as they fall due

rubric: Asset composition matters; slow receivables and inventory are less liquid than cash.
Distractors accept the headline ratio without judging composition.

items.prompt: You are judging whether a firm's reported earnings quality is high. Which findings count as red flags that earnings may be overstated relative to underlying performance? Select all that apply.

options.label: Receivables growing much faster than revenue over several periods
Operating cash flow consistently exceeding net income by a stable margin
Capitalizing of routine operating costs rising as a share of capex
Gross margin steady while sales grow in line with the industry

rubric: Receivables outpacing sales and cost capitalization can inflate earnings.
Stable cash above income and steady margins are not warning signs.

items.prompt: An analyst compares two airlines. Airline P has a 4% net margin and a debt/EBITDA of 1.5. Airline Q has a 9% net margin, debt/EBITDA of 4.5, and fuel hedges that expire next year. Criterion: resilience to a fuel price spike over two years. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Q is more resilient, because hedges that expire show the firm already managed its fuel exposure
Q is more resilient, since its higher margin provides a buffer that outweighs leverage and hedge expiry
P is more resilient, because lower leverage leaves more room to absorb a squeeze once Q's hedges expire
P and Q are equally resilient, because a fuel spike hits both through the same fuel cost line

rubric: Q's high leverage plus expiring hedges makes it fragile to a cost shock.
Distractors overweight current margin or treat expiring hedges as protection.

items.prompt: You must design a covenant package for a lender to a cyclical firm. It must stay meaningful in downturns, resist accounting manipulation, and reflect cash servicing capacity. Which is the best design?

options.label: Minimum current ratio of 1.5, tested at each year end on audited accounts, with a cure right through equity injection
Minimum fixed-charge coverage on EBITDA less capex and taxes, tested quarterly on a trailing 12-month basis
Maximum debt/equity of 2.0 on book values, tested quarterly, with goodwill and intangibles excluded from equity
Minimum net income of a fixed amount, tested on each reported quarter, with adjustments for one-off items

rubric: Cash-based coverage over trailing periods smooths cyclicality and limits manipulation.
Distractors use book or accrual measures that are easily managed or volatile.

items.prompt: You are building a model to forecast a growing retailer's cash needs. Constraints: it must link to the three statements, capture seasonality, and show whether growth is self-funded. Which design is best?

options.label: Forecast net income from a fixed margin each year, add back depreciation, and treat the result as cash available to fund growth
Forecast the income statement quarterly with seasonal revenue, and assume ending cash equals prior cash plus net income each quarter
Project revenue, drive receivables, inventory and payables by days metrics monthly, and balance the sheet with a revolver
Grow every balance sheet line at the revenue growth rate each year, link net income to equity, and solve cash as the balancing plug

rubric: Driver-based monthly working capital with a revolver captures seasonality and funding needs.
Distractors skip integration or seasonality.

items.prompt: Design a peer-comparison method for a company using IFRS against peers using US GAAP, with different lease and inventory methods. It must be consistent and not hide the differences. Which is best?

options.label: Compare revenue growth and operating margins as reported, since both are mostly unaffected by lease and inventory choices
Rank peers by reported net income, and disclose each peer's accounting standard and inventory method in a footnote
Restate peers to a common lease and inventory basis, and reconcile each adjustment to reported figures
Use the largest peer's reported ratios as the benchmark, and scale the other peers' figures to match its policies

rubric: Normalizing to a common basis with reconciliations keeps comparability transparent.
Distractors ignore or merely footnote differences.

items.prompt: You need a distress early-warning screen for a mid-sized supplier portfolio. It must use public statements, avoid single-ratio reliance, and flag deteriorating trends before covenant breaches. Which is the best build?

options.label: Rank suppliers by revenue size each year and flag the smallest quartile as the riskiest group, since scale predicts survival
A flag triggered when net income turns negative in any single year, since a reported loss is the clearest sign of distress
A composite of coverage, liquidity, cash flow and leverage ratios with trend thresholds, checked against past defaults
A single threshold on the current ratio, recalculated each year from audited statements and set by industry norms

rubric: Multi-factor trend-based scoring gives earlier, more robust warnings.
Distractors rely on one lagging measure or size.

items.prompt: Design an adjustment to compare two firms whose profits are distorted by one-off items. Constraints: avoid cherry-picking, keep recurring costs in, and be repeatable across years. Which is best?

options.label: Use the figure management labels as adjusted earnings, since management knows best which items in each year are unusual and non-operating
Exclude all restructuring charges every year for both firms and report the cleaned earnings as the recurring operating figure for comparison
Remove any expense that exceeds 5% of revenue in a year for both firms, since items that large are probably one-off rather than operating
Apply written criteria for non-recurring items, test frequency over five years, and treat repeating charges as operating

rubric: Rule-based criteria and frequency testing prevent cherry-picking.
Distractors accept labels or exclude recurring charges.

items.prompt: You are designing a quality-of-earnings review for an acquisition target. It must test whether reported profit converts to cash and whether it is recurring. Which components should it include? Select all that apply.

options.label: Relying on the seller's adjusted EBITDA schedule without independent testing
Comparing only the latest year to avoid noise from earlier periods
Analysis of revenue recognition timing and deferred revenue changes across periods
Reconciling EBITDA to operating cash flow, with working capital movements isolated

rubric: Cash reconciliation and revenue timing analysis test conversion and recurrence.
Seller schedules unchecked and single-year views defeat the objective.

items.prompt: A board wants a single capital-structure policy for a firm with volatile cash flows. It must keep access to credit in a downturn, limit refinancing risk, and not forgo all growth. Which policy best meets every constraint?

options.label: Use only equity and hold no debt, so financial risk is eliminated and all growth is funded by issuing new shares at market prices
Target net debt/EBITDA stress-tested on a downturn case, with staggered maturities and a committed undrawn facility
Match all debt to short-term maturities, so rates reset quickly and interest costs stay low whenever policy rates fall
Maximize debt up to covenant limits to boost ROE, refinancing everything at once whenever market rates drop below coupons

rubric: Stress-tested leverage, laddered maturities and committed liquidity meet all constraints.
Distractors ignore refinancing risk or growth.
